observation: Transaction throughput is critically affected by the order in which conflicting transactions execute, yet practical systems generally process transactions in FIFO order and resolve conflicts reactively, and recent scheduling techniques explore only a small subset of possible schedules. The resulting performance gap is large and systematic: for a batch of four conflicting transactions one schedule can reduce makespan by 25% over another, the gap grows arbitrarily for larger workloads, and on real workload traces FIFO can increase makespan over optimized schedules by 43.2% for Epinions, 8.0% for SmallBank, 96.2% for TAOBench, 101.6% for TPC-C, and 99.3% for YCSB. Finding an optimal schedule is NP-complete, and existing heuristics sacrifice schedule quality for efficiency.

solution.idea: The observation shows that schedule choice is a large, systematic performance variable, yet every existing layer treats order as an emergent artifact: reactive protocols let lock waits and timestamps decide the serialization order, deterministic databases inherit the order of a replication/submission queue, and empirical deterministic studies evaluate only fixed ordering heuristics. The NP-completeness result explains why no one searches the schedule space exactly: exact optimization is impractical for large batches. The missing piece is a scheduling layer that (1) makes order an explicit, controllable decision at a point where the chosen order can actually be enforced, and (2) treats schedule optimization as an anytime, model-based search rather than as either a trivial heuristic or an exact exponential procedure. The direction I choose is therefore a batch order optimizer sitting between transaction admission and the deterministic sequencing/execution layer. It collects a short batch of transactions with predeclared read/write sets, builds an explicit conflict graph, scores candidate orders with a shadow-execution cost model estimating batch makespan, and searches that order space with a time-bounded portfolio: exact dynamic programming for small conflict components, and large-neighborhood search plus iterated local search for large components. The core insight is to separate the two difficult subproblems: predicting the makespan of an order, and finding a low-makespan order. The first is handled by a calibrated shadow estimator, the second by an anytime search whose quality improves with available time. This directly attacks the observation: FIFO and timestamp orders correspond to exploring exactly one schedule, while greedier constructive heuristics explore only a small neighborhood of that one schedule; our search explicitly samples, recombines, and improves many qualitatively different schedules in the batch. The key trade-off is optimization time versus schedule quality, and we make that trade-off explicit and tunable instead of hiding it inside a fixed heuristic. An exact global search was rejected because it cannot scale beyond small instances; a pure heuristic was rejected because the observation demonstrates large systematic gaps; learned/RL approaches were considered but rejected because they require training data and exploration in a live transactional system, whereas the model-based anytime optimizer is immediately deployable and improves its schedule as the time budget grows.
solution.implementation:
The implementation is a scheduler component inserted before the deterministic sequence generator. It receives transaction descriptors (read set R, write set W, estimated per-record service times, and whether the transaction is short/long). The component runs in a tight loop with four modules: batch assembly, conflict-graph construction, cost evaluation, and anytime search.

1. Batch assembly: Incoming descriptors wait in an admission queue. A batch is formed when either (a) the queue reaches max_batch_size (default 64), or (b) a timer reaches batch_timeout (default 1 ms). When a batch is ready, it is frozen; transactions arriving during the batch's search are held for the next batch. The previous batch is still executing while the current batch is searched, so optimization time is mostly hidden.

2. Conflict graph: For each key in R and W, an inverted index maps the key to the list of transactions accessing it. Two transactions receive a conflict edge if they access a common key and at least one of them writes it. Each transaction also carries an estimated isolated execution time p_t computed by an online profiler from past executions of the same stored procedure form. The conflict graph is partitioned into connected components, because transactions in different components do not conflict and can be optimized independently; the makespan of a batch is then the maximum makespan over components under the shadow-execution model. Components with one vertex are skipped.

3. Cost evaluation: The function shadow_cost(pi, component) estimates the makespan if the component's transactions are executed in the total order pi. A shadow executor plays the order against a lightweight event model of the deterministic engine. For each transaction t in the order and each key k in R_t union W_t, the model tracks the last commit time of any earlier transaction in pi that conflicts with t on k. Transaction t cannot obtain k before that time. It also tracks per-partition worker availability. The transaction's projected start time is the maximum over (a) all conflicting lock tail times for keys it needs, and (b) the earliest time a worker is free at the partition that owns its home key. Its projected completion time is start plus p_t plus a small per-key serialization/transition cost calibrated by the profiler. After the projected completion, all locks of t are released and per-key tail times advance. shadow_cost is used only on finalists and on components with small size; during search, a faster surrogate cost is used: it builds the same dependency DAG but ignores worker availability and uses per-key tail times only. The surrogate is periodically recalibrated to the full shadow model.

4. Anytime search: For each conflict component, if n <= exact_limit (default 14), run exact dynamic-programming search over subsets of transactions. The DP state is (subset, last transaction); it stores the minimal projected completion time of ordering the subset with that last element. The recurrence extends each subset by every remaining transaction and uses the surrogate cost to compute the new completion. This returns a proven optimal order for that component. For larger components, run a general anytime search composed of the following steps. First, generate a set of seeds: (a) original FIFO order, (b) shortest-transaction-first, (c) most-conflicting-first, (d) least-conflicting-first, and (e) a random permutation. For each seed, run iterated local search. The primary neighborhood moves are: move a transaction to every other position; swap two non-adjacent transactions; and reverse a sub-sequence. Each move is evaluated incrementally with the surrogate by recomputing only the affected portions of the dependency DAG. For small movements this takes O(delta) time where delta is the number of conflict edges involving the moved transactions. The search accepts improving moves; after a local optimum, it performs a destroy/repair perturbation: remove a contiguous or conflict-dense subsequence of size floor(n / 4), then reinsert the removed transactions one at a time at the position that minimizes the current surrogate cost plus a regret term for later insertions. The perturbed solution becomes the new starting point, and the process repeats. A simulated-annealing acceptance rule allows occasional uphill moves early in the search, with temperature cooling over the allotted time. A shared elite set of the best distinct orders is maintained; at the end, every elite order is evaluated with the full shadow model, and the one with the smallest estimated makespan is chosen.

5. Search budget allocation: The scheduler is given a global time budget per batch. The budget is initially estimated as a fraction of the previous batch's shadow makespan, clipped to min_search_time and max_search_time. Within that budget, connected components are searched by decreasing total estimated workload. If a component search finishes early and finds a proven optimum, its unused budget is transferred to the next-largest component.

6. Integration and quality control: The chosen order is emitted to the deterministic sequence generator for all replicas. For non-deterministic engines, the same order can be used as a preference order in the lock manager: each transaction receives a sequence ticket, and lock requests are granted in ticket order whenever doing so does not introduce deadlock; however, the strong guarantee is only in deterministic execution. After the batch executes, the profiler updates p_t and transition-cost estimates with measured durations. If the shadow model's prediction for the executed batch differs from the actual makespan by more than a threshold (default 20%), the profiler increases the cost-model influence of recent measurements and the search uses a shorter batch size on the next few batches to reduce model uncertainty. The implementation exposes parameters exact_limit, max_batch_size, batch_timeout, min/max search time, and a quality-versus-latency knob that scales search time linearly with batch conflict density. This design gives an engineer all pieces needed to implement the optimizer: an admission/reorder buffer, a conflict graph, a shadow makespan estimator, a surrogate score, a DP for small components, and an LNS/ILS loop for large components, with online calibration closing the loop.
